prize_parts.citation: for their theoretical analyses of how special-interest politics shapes trade policy, and of how trade, innovation and growth interact

statement.case_for: Grossman and Helpman turned the question of why trade policy departs from efficiency into a tractable, testable framework. The protection-for-sale model and the book on interest groups and trade policy explain tariff formation as an equilibrium of lobbying and government objectives. The same pair's work on innovation and growth in the global economy extends the contribution beyond trade. The credit is unusually clean: a long, tightly coupled joint record, a two-name configuration and no obvious omitted co-originator at the same level. The core results are three decades old, so they have been through extensive testing, extension and textbook absorption. The ranking summary shows nine members placing this entry in their top three, so the colleagues' written assessments I read converge on its attribution and maturity. That convergence is not itself evidence of merit. I rest the case on those written assessments of attribution, maturity and influence, which match my own reading.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is empirical. Estimates of the structural parameters in the protection-for-sale equilibrium are sensitive to specification, and support for its predictions is mixed. The contribution is therefore more a disciplined framework that changed how the field reasons than a settled empirical result. A second concern is that trade was recognised in 2008 and the 2025 prize covered innovation-led growth, so the committee must be satisfied that this is a distinct advance. Helpman's presence on B030 also means the committee must decide which trade strand it is rewarding.

responses.point: Hjalmarsson ranks the Autor-Hanson-Katz labour and trade-shock entry first. She values the combination of credible designs with an explanatory framework, and she places the protection-for-sale framework third, noting that its empirical testing is mixed and that the trade field has been recognised before.
responses.response: I agree that B018 has stronger design-based evidence and larger recent policy reach, and I ranked it third. Two things keep me from moving it ahead. Attribution is less clean: the task framework has originators outside the credited names, Acemoglu among them, and Katz would be a fourth name beyond what a three-name proposal allows. The persistence of the China-shock effects and the shift-share identification are also still being worked through. Her point about mixed empirical support for protection-for-sale is fair, and I concede it. But a framework that organised three decades of theory and testing, even where some tests disagree, seems to me a mature contribution. I keep B018 as an alternative rather than the preferred part.

responses.point: Krusell ranks the BLP and dynamic-oligopoly entry first because it is standard in merger review, antitrust and regulation, and he flags that the committee may prefer a substantive discovery to a method. He also notes the Bresnahan-versus-Levinsohn choice within the three-name cap.
responses.response: I ranked B002 second and take his case seriously. Its practical reach is very large, and I disclose below that it is my own field, so I discount my enthusiasm. My reservations are attribution and framing. BLP is clearly Berry, Levinsohn and Pakes, but Bresnahan and Reiss laid the empirical-IO foundations and Pakes's dynamic-games work is a separate strand. Identification debates between structural and design-based approaches also remain open. B001 has a tighter credit structure, and I would not call B002 weaker on merit. If the committee wants an applied-methods prize, I would support a BLP triple as the next best configuration.

responses.point: Teorell ranks B001 first but notes that empirical support for protection-for-sale is mixed. He also raises that the committee might prefer to anchor a trade prize on another strand, such as firm heterogeneity, which would change the credited set.
responses.response: I share the caveat about empirical support and have recorded it as my main reservation. On firm heterogeneity, I ranked B030 seventh. Melitz's contribution is a single pivotal paper. The exporter facts were established earlier and independently by Bernard, Eaton, Jensen and Kortum, none of whom is credited there, so its attribution is the weaker of the two trade entries. Choosing B001 does not preclude later recognition of the firm-level strand. I would resist building a trade prize around B030 as it is currently credited.

responses.point: Boppart ranks the Obstfeld-Rogoff open-economy entry first and Melitz-Helpman second, and he notes that Helpman appears on both B001 and B030, which could split support.
responses.response: The split risk is real, but I treat it as a procedural matter and not as evidence against either contribution. I place B001 above B030 because the Grossman-Helpman credit is cleaner, with two names and no important uncredited co-originator at the same level. On B003, the intertemporal framework is well attributed to Obstfeld and Rogoff, and I ranked it fourth. I give less weight to it than he does because several of the puzzles it names remain unresolved, so part of the entry is a research agenda rather than a settled result.

uncertainties: How much weight the committee should place on the mixed empirical record of the protection-for-sale equilibrium relative to its influence on theory and applied work.
Whether the citation should centre on the political economy of trade policy alone or also name the innovation-growth-trade strand, which the shortlist entry's stated discovery does not emphasise.
Whether recognition in 2008 (trade) and 2025 (innovation-led growth) makes the committee less receptive to a trade-and-growth citation.
How a vote split between B001 and B030 over Helpman would affect the outcome, and whether that should influence the configuration.
I have not independently verified citation or impact figures and rely on the written assessments in the supplied evidence.
statement.conflict_note: No connection to Helpman or Grossman is apparent from my supplied profile. For completeness, I have co-authored with committee chair John Hassler and former chair Tore Ellingsen (IJIO 2026), and my profile lists a co-author at Chicago Booth, Chad Syverson. None of these links is to a credited name in B001. My field is industrial organisation and trade, so I may weigh B002 and the trade entries more heavily than colleagues, and I have tried to apply the same criteria across fields. The public fact that I am married to a former Swedish prime minister is noted only for completeness. It has no apparent bearing on any shortlisted candidate.
